string.text: In 1715, the Aniyvwiya Confederacy—historically known to Europeans as the Cherokee Nation—was at a pivotal turning point in its history, occupying a vast and historically peak territory across the southern Appalachian region. While the confederacy shared a deeply rooted matriarchal structure, common language, and ceremonial unity, political authority remained highly decentralized and town-based. The year 1715 was defined by the outbreak of the Yamasee War, a massive pan-Indigenous uprising against the colony of South Carolina sparked by British trading abuses and land encroachments.

The Kingdom of Great Britain was a sovereign state in Western Europe from 1707 to the end of 1800. The state was created by the 1706 Treaty of Union and ratified by the Acts of Union 1707, which united the kingdoms of England (which included Wales) and Scotland to form a single kingdom encompassing the whole island of Great Britain and its outlying islands, with the exception of the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands. The unitary state was governed by a single parliament at the Palace of Westminster, but distinct legal systems—English law and Scots law—remained in use.

New France was the territory colonized by France in North America, beginning with the exploration of the Gulf of Saint Lawrence by Jacques Cartier in 1534 and ending with the cession of New France to Great Britain and Spain in 1763 under the Treaty of Paris. A vast viceroyalty, New France consisted of five colonies at its peak in 1712, each with its own administration: Canada, the most developed colony, which was divided into the districts of Quebec, Trois-Rivières, and Montreal; Hudson Bay; Acadia in the northeast; Terre-Neuve on the island of Newfoundland; and Louisiana. It extended from Newfoundland to the Canadian Prairies and from Hudson Bay to the Gulf of Mexico, including all the Great Lakes of North America. The continent-traversing Saint Lawrence and Mississippi rivers were means of carrying French influence through much of North America.

The Haudenosaunee Confederacy in 1715 was a powerful Five Nations alliance composed of the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca, operating at a critical geopolitical turning point under the Great Law of Peace. At this time, the Confederacy was actively navigating the complex diplomatic waters of the Beaver Wars' aftermath, maintaining strategic neutrality between British and French colonial empires to protect its sovereign fur-trade interests and territory.

By 1715, the Illinois Confederacy—a once-mighty alliance of Algonquian-speaking Native American tribes—faced severe demographic and territorial pressures, reducing its composition from roughly a dozen tribes to five primary groups: the Kaskaskia, Cahokia, Peoria, Tamaroa, and Michigamea. Decimated by European diseases and grueling conflicts like the Beaver Wars against the Iroquois, the remaining populations had increasingly consolidated and shifted southward into the Mississippi River Valley.

Cudjoe's Town was located in the mountains in the southern extremities of the parish of St James, close to the border of Westmoreland, Jamaica.In 1690 a large number of Akan freedom fighters already living in the mountains launched an assault on the Sutton's Estate in Clarendon, central Jamaica, free between 300 and 400 enslaved people. They established a new town of Free black people in Jamaica, in the forested mountains of the island's interior, in the Cockpit Country. Naquan, Cudjoe's father, was allegedly the one who orchestrated this rebellion. Naquan was succeeded by Cudjoe, the first leader of this group of Jamaican Maroons in western Jamaica.

The Muscogee were a confederacy of tribes consisting of Yuchi, Koasati, Alabama, Coosa, Tuskegee, Coweta, Cusseta, Chehaw (Chiaha), Hitchiti, Tuckabatchee, Oakfuskee, and many others. The basic social unit was the town (idalwa). Abihka, Coosa, Tuckabutche, and Coweta are the four mother towns of the Muscogee Confederacy. Traditionally, the Cusseta and Coweta bands are considered the earliest members of the Muscogee Nation.

Nassau was then taken over by English privateers, who became completely lawless pirates over time. The pirates attacked French and Spanish ships, while the French and Spanish forces burned Nassau several more times. Pirates established themselves in Nassau, and essentially established their own republic with its own governors. By 1713, the War of the Spanish Succession was over, but many British privateers were slow to get the news, or reluctant to accept it, and so slipped into piracy. This led to large numbers of unemployed privateers making their way to New Providence to join the republic and swell its numbers.

In 1715, the Saawanwaki (Shawnee) Confederacy operated not as a strictly centralized empire, but as a fluid network of highly autonomous, Algonquian-speaking subdivisions—including the Chillicothe, Hathawekela, Kispokotha, Mequachake, and Piqua—who were dispersed across North America due to geopolitical pressures like the Beaver Wars. Driven by their unique, migratory nature, various bands of the Shawnee established strategic settlements from Pennsylvania and the Ohio Valley down to the American Southeast. A critical turning point for the southern branches occurred in April 1715 with the outbreak of the Yamasee War in South Carolina.

The Seven Council Fires refers to Očhéthi Šakówiŋ, a collective term for the Great Sioux Nation, which comprises seven oyates (nations or people): the Lakota (Thítȟuŋwaŋ), the four Eastern Dakota bands (Bdewákaŋthuŋwaŋ, Waȟpéthuŋwaŋ, Waȟpékhute, and Sisíthuŋwaŋ), and the two Western Dakota bands (Iháŋkthuŋwaŋ and Iháŋkthuŋwaŋna). The fires in the name represent the seven distinct peoples who make up this confederacy.
The Council of the Three Fires

In 1715, the Council of the Three Fires—a long-standing Anishinaabe alliance comprising the Ojibwe (Keepers of the Faith), Odawa (Keepers of the Trade), and Potawatomi (Keepers of the Fire)—faced critical shifts in regional diplomacy and conflict during the First Fox War. Centred strategically around Michilimackinac, the confederacy increasingly adapted its military and trade networks to balance relations with European powers.

By 1715, the Wabanaki Confederacy was navigating a highly volatile geopolitical landscape in the aftermath of Queen Anne’s War and the 1713 Treaty of Utrecht. Frustrated that the European treaty had ceded their ancestral lands in Acadia to the British Crown without their consent, member nations like the Mi'kmaq and Abenaki actively resisted aggressive British expansion into present-day Maine and Nova Scotia

The Wabash Confederacy emerged as a fluid, multi-tribal alliance primarily composed of the Miami, Wea, and Piankashaw nations, alongside smaller groups like the Kickapoo and Mascouten. Centered along the strategically vital Wabash River valley in modern-day Indiana and Illinois, this confederacy was not a centralized nation-state but rather a loose political network of influential village headmen and chiefs who united to manage regional trade and defense.
